```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
library(tidyverse)
```

The Module 4 project uses RNA sequencing of
1,306,127 individual cells from the brains of two mouse embryos provided by 10x Genomics.

# Source

10x Genomics, a company that makes single-cell sequencing instruments,
released the data in 2017. The cells come from the cortex, hippocampus and subventricular zone of
two mice (strain C57BL/6) at embryonic day 18, a few days before birth.

- The dataset page, with a description of the experiment and all the files:
  [1.3 Million Brain Cells from E18 Mice](https://www.10xgenomics.com/datasets/1-3-million-brain-cells-from-e-18-mice-2-standard-1-3-0)
- The full count matrix, 4.2 GB in HDF5 format:
  [1M_neurons_filtered_gene_bc_matrices_h5.h5](https://cf.10xgenomics.com/samples/cell-exp/1.3.0/1M_neurons/1M_neurons_filtered_gene_bc_matrices_h5.h5)
- 10x's random subsample of 20,000 cells:
  [1M_neurons_neuron20k.h5](https://cf.10xgenomics.com/samples/cell-exp/1.3.0/1M_neurons/1M_neurons_neuron20k.h5)
- 10x's automated analysis, including the cluster labels:
  [1M_neurons_analysis.tar.gz](https://cf.10xgenomics.com/samples/cell-exp/1.3.0/1M_neurons/1M_neurons_analysis.tar.gz)
- A copy at the Human Cell Atlas data portal, which hosts some mouse
  datasets alongside its human ones:
  [1M Neurons](https://explore.data.humancellatlas.org/projects/74b6d569-3b11-42ef-b6b1-a0454522b4a0)
- Background on the method:
  [single-cell transcriptomics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single-cell_transcriptomics) on Wikipedia

The data are licensed
[CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/): you may use and
share them, with credit to 10x Genomics.

# Measurements

A cell makes RNA copies of the genes it is using. The 10x instrument wraps
each cell in its own tiny **droplet** of oil, together with a bead carrying a
unique barcode. Every RNA molecule from that cell is tagged with the barcode,
so after sequencing each molecule can be traced to its cell, and the
molecules from each of 27,998 mouse genes can be counted in each cell. A cell's counts say which genes it is using, and so what kind of
cell it is: a neuron uses different genes from a dividing stem cell.

- Most counts are zero. A typical cell has molecules from about 1,900 genes.
- Counting misses most molecules, so a zero does not mean the gene is unused.
  A missed gene is called a **dropout**.
- The total number of molecules counted in a cell is its **library size**. It
  depends on the cell's size and on how well its RNA was captured, so counts
  are usually compared relative to it.
- The cells were sequenced in 133 separate runs (**batches**). Cells in the
  same run were processed together, so they can differ from cells in other
  runs for reasons that have nothing to do with biology.
- A droplet that captured two cells (a **doublet**) looks like one cell with
  about twice the RNA and a mix of both cells' genes.

# Data Cleaning

The full data are 1,306,127 cells by 27,998 genes, too large to work with on a
laptop. We made two smaller files from them.

- **`brain_cells` keeps every cell but only a few genes.** For each cell we
  computed the library size, the number of genes detected and the
  mitochondrial count from all 27,998 genes, then kept the counts of 30 marker
  genes and dropped the rest.
- **`brain_genes` keeps many genes but fewer cells.** It uses the 20,000
  cells 10x chose at random, and the 2,000 genes that vary most
  across them.
- **We added labels.** Each cell's barcode ends in the number of its run,
  which became `batch`. 10x's cluster labels were matched to cells by barcode.
- **We renamed some genes.** R does not allow `-` in a column name, so
  `Hba-a1` is `Hba.a1`. Names that start with a digit get an `X` in front,
  and a few duplicated names end in `.1`.

# Files

In the course `data/` folder you will find compressed CSV files that can be read using `read.csv` (no need to decompress manually).

## `brain_cells.csv.gz`


```{r cells}
cells <- read.csv("../../data/brain_cells.csv.gz")
dim(cells)
```
Rows are cells.

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `cell` | 1 to 1,306,127, the cell's position in the 10x file |
| `batch` | which of the 133 sequencing runs the cell came from |
| `library` | total molecules counted in the cell, over all genes |
| `detected` | number of genes with at least one molecule counted |
| `mito` | molecules from the 13 mitochondrial genes |
| `graph` | 10x's graph-based cluster, 1 to 60, numbered largest first |
| `kmeans10` | 10x's k-means cluster, with 10 clusters |
| 30 gene columns | molecules counted for each of 30 marker genes |

The 30 genes are known markers of kinds of cells in the developing brain:

[Mouse Genome Informatics](https://www.informatics.jax.org/) describes
what each gene does.

```{r marker-table, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
marks <- list(
  c("Stmn2", "Snap25", "Tubb3"), "neurons",
  c("Neurod6", "Slc17a6", "Tbr1", "Satb2", "Bcl11b"), "excitatory neurons",
  c("Gad1", "Gad2", "Dlx2", "Lhx6"), "inhibitory neurons",
  "Reln", "Cajal-Retzius cells, early neurons on the brain's surface",
  "Eomes", "intermediate progenitors, which divide to make neurons",
  c("Pax6", "Sox2", "Hes5", "Fabp7", "Nes"), "radial glia, the brain's stem cells",
  c("Mki67", "Top2a"), "any dividing cell",
  c("Olig2", "Pdgfra"), "oligodendrocyte precursors",
  "Aqp4", "astrocytes",
  "C1qa", "microglia, the brain's immune cells",
  "Cldn5", "cells lining blood vessels",
  c("Hba.a1", "Hbb.bs"), "hemoglobin: red blood cells, a contaminant",
  "Xist", "X inactivation; made only by female cells",
  "Malat1", "a highly expressed RNA found in nearly every cell")
link <- function(g) {
  if (!knitr::is_html_output()) return(sprintf("`%s`", g))
  sprintf("[`%s`](https://www.informatics.jax.org/quicksearch/summary?queryType=exactPhrase&query=%s)",
          g, sub(".", "-", g, fixed = TRUE))
}
genes_col <- sapply(marks[c(TRUE, FALSE)], \(g) paste(link(g), collapse = ", "))
cat("| Genes | Usually marks |\n|---|---|\n")
cat(sprintf("| %s | %s |\n", genes_col, unlist(marks[c(FALSE, TRUE)])), sep = "")
```

## `brain_genes.csv.gz`

```{r genes}
genes <- read.csv("../../data/brain_genes.csv.gz")
dim(genes)
```

These are the 20,000 cells of 10x's random subsample. The first five columns
are `cell`, `batch`, `library`, `graph` and `kmeans10`, as in `brain_cells`; `cell`
matches the same column of `brain_cells`. The other 2,000 columns count
molecules for 2,000 **highly variable** genes. These were chosen among the
genes counted in at least 1% of the 20,000 cells, as the 2,000 whose value of
$\log(1 + 10000 \times \text{count} / \text{library})$ varies most across
cells. Seventeen of the 30 marker genes are among them.

# Notes

- **The clusters are automated labels.** 10x found `graph` and `kmeans10` by
  clustering the cells on their first 20 principal components, with no
  biologist involved. They may or may not correspond to kinds of cells.
- **The sample appears to be female.** `Xist` is counted in 96% of cells, and
  `Ddx3y`, a gene on the Y chromosome, is never counted. A cell with no
  `Xist` is a dropout, not a male cell.
- **The cells are not independent.** Cells from the same batch, and from the
  same mouse, share conditions.
